practice_questions.text:
A sewing machine needle moves up and down in a straight line repeatedly. What type of motion is this?
A) Rotary
B) Linear
C) Reciprocating
D) Oscillating
Identify the type of motion produced by a pendulum clock's pendulum.
Describe how a rack and pinion mechanism converts one type of motion into another.
practice_questions.marks:
• A circular pinion gear meshes with a flat, toothed bar called a rack. [1 mark]
• As the pinion rotates (rotary motion), it moves along the teeth of the rack. [1 mark]
• This causes the rack to slide in a straight line, converting rotary motion into linear motion. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the three classes of lever and give one example product for each.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per correct class with example:
• First-order: fulcrum between load and effort — e.g. seesaw, scissors, crow bar.
• Second-order: load between fulcrum and effort — e.g. wheelbarrow, bottle opener, nutcracker.
• Third-order: effort between fulcrum and load — e.g. tweezers, fishing rod, forearm. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a cam and follower system is used in a mechanical toy to make a figure wave its arm up and down. State the type of motion produced at each stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A motor provides rotary motion, turning the cam about its central axis.
• The cam is off-centre (eccentric) or pear-shaped, so its surface rises and falls as it rotates.
• The follower rests on the cam surface and is pushed up and down, producing reciprocating motion.
• This reciprocating motion is linked to the figure's arm to create the waving action.
[4 marks: 1 per clear point]

practice_questions.text: A designer is choosing between a gear system and a belt-and-pulley system to drive the drum of a washing machine from an electric motor. Compare the two systems, discussing their suitability for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear system:
• Gears mesh directly via teeth; no slip possible — positive drive, reliable speed ratio.
• More expensive to manufacture with high precision; noisier in operation.
• Suitable where exact speed ratios must be maintained.
Belt-and-pulley system:
• Relies on friction between belt and pulley; can slip if overloaded (acts as safety release).
• Cheaper, quieter, and able to transmit drive over longer distances between shafts.
• Belts can stretch or snap over time — maintenance required.
• Most domestic washing machines use a belt drive because it is quieter and cheaper; the slip under overload protects the motor.
[5 marks — 1 mark per developed comparison point up to 5. A fully developed answer must address both systems with context of the washing machine.]
